stories.headline: Lakshya Raichandani dedicates U19 Asia Cup glory to his late coach
stories.deck: Lakshya’s reverence for high-class batsmanship is also reflected in his admiration for Joe Root and Virat Kohli. “I love Root and Kohli. I love their game sense and playing style,” he said
stories.bodyText:
The opening batter, fresh from leading the nation to glory in the U19 Asia Cup in Oman, isn’t just saying it because it appears to be the right thing to say.
His penchant for the classical format shines through in his orthodoxy at the top of the order. Sample his knock of 80 off 101 balls against Pakistan in the final on Saturday (November 14, 2026), where he prioritised impeccable timing over brute force and caressed the ball along the turf for his boundaries.
Since returning home to Gonda in Uttar Pradesh, Lakshya has been flooded with congratulatory calls and messages. “It is yet to sink in. It will take a bit more time. But it is a great feeling,” Lakshya told The Hindu.
The 18-year-old had endured a personal setback last month when his coach, Abhishek Mishra, passed away at the age of 40. The continental title has provided some solace. “I dedicate this victory to my coach,” he said.
If Lakshya’s maturity belies his age, his steely upbringing has played a role. He was all of 10 when his parents sent him away to neighbouring Uttarakhand for his cricketing education.
“Lakshya moved to Rudrapur for two years and Haldwani thereafter to train under his coach. He has lived in hostels since then. We sent him with a heavy heart. He is our younger son. It was difficult at first, but we gradually adjusted,” his father Rajesh Raichandani, a businessman and politician with ties to the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), stated.
The hilly terrains of Uttarakhand, the State that Lakshya represents in domestic cricket, helped the batter hone his technique against the moving ball.
“Where we play up north, the ball swings a fair bit. You need a solid technique to deal with that. I believe in playing according to the situation. I can change gears at any moment. I have the full range of strokes to play all formats,” he declared.
Lakshya’s reverence for high-class batsmanship is also reflected in his admiration for Joe Root and Virat Kohli. “I love Root and Kohli. I love their game sense and playing style,” he said.
In his young career, Lakshya, who has already played seven Ranji Trophy fixtures for Uttarakhand, has shown the propensity to chalk up big scores. In India u-19’s four-day games this year, he hit 207 against Sri Lanka in July and 240 versus Australia in September.
What is the secret sauce behind these returns?
“Just have to keep it simple. Focus on one ball at a time,” he opined. “You should know how to switch on and switch off in order to focus for a long time at the crease. I like to switch off by walking towards the square-leg umpire after every ball and then switch on with a trigger word like ‘focus’ or ‘one ball at a time’ to get back into the zone.”

Back-channel negotiations, informal meetings and intense lobbying are gathering momentum ahead of the December 5 polls, with multiple camps working to consolidate support and shape the presidential contest.
Olympic medallist Gagan Narang has emerged as a frontrunner for the president’s post, with sources indicating that his candidature has backing from within the government. Rajeev Mehta
, amid concerns over the extent of govt influence in the Olympic body. Adding another dimension to the contest is the return in the fray of incumbent president 
PT Usha

Sources said an informal meeting on the sidelines of the recently held sports day awards discussed Narang’s candidature, alongside other possible appointments. Sources indicated Usha could either contest independently or extend support to an NSF-backed candidate, potentially avoiding a three-way contest.

stories.headline: Sachin Tendulkar donates 25 bats, and the stories that came with them
stories.bodyText:
“I’ve said that it (the cricket bat) is an extension of my body. So, I’m giving you a part of my body. Please take care of it.”
For Sachin Tendulkar, a cricket bat was never just equipment. It was a companion through a 24-year career, a source of runs and, at times, reassurance. The 25 bats he handed over to the MCA Sharad Pawar Cricket Museum on Monday, in the presence of MCA president Ajinkya Naik, told the story – from an unexpected childhood gift to the bat he used in his final Test innings against West Indies at Wankhede Stadium in 2013.
Titled Batography, the collection is more than a display of memorabilia. Each bat marks a moment in Tendulkar’s journey and offers a glimpse into his personal choices and beliefs. His association with bats began when he was five, after his sister brought him one from Kashmir.
“My sister Savita Tai had gone on a trip to Kashmir. I was expecting her to bring back walnuts, apples and other things. But when she gifted me a cricket bat instead, I was absolutely delighted. From then on, that bat accompanied me everywhere,” he recalled at a fireside chat on Monday.
His brother Ajit and coach Ramakant Achrekar later helped him get his first season-ball bat: a full-size Symonds, heavy for a 12-year-old.
“In 1985, I received my first leather-ball bat. I had gone with Achrekar Sir, and the moment I saw a particular bat, I liked it and decided that I wanted that one. From the sixth standard onwards, I started concentrating seriously on cricket. My elder brother spoke to my father, who then bought me a separate bat. It was a full-sized bat and quite heavy for my age, but I was determined to have that particular bat.”
As an adult, his choices also reflected the values he carried from home. During the 1996 World Cup, Tendulkar played with a sponsorless bat because his family had decided he would not promote alcohol or tobacco.
“At home, we had decided – the whole family had decided – that I would never promote alcohol or tobacco,” he said. “I ended up playing for close to two years without any sticker on my bat.”
A foreign sports brand offered him a deal during the tournament. But having already played two matches without a sticker, including a hundred against Kenya, Tendulkar was reluctant to change anything.
“I said, ‘No. I’m slightly superstitious now. With the blank bat, it was priceless to score those runs. We’ll talk after the World Cup is over.’ Right now, the whole World Cup, I’m going to play with a blank bat.”
Another bat had an unusual journey into his collection. In 2009, Soni Kohli showed him a bat in Mohali that had been made for former India spinner Sunil Joshi. Tendulkar liked it, and it was delivered as the team bus was leaving for the Hyderabad match against Australia.
“I hadn’t played a single ball with it. I took it out and played with it in the match. A brand-new bat,” he said.
The bat soon became a favourite. He used it to score 175 against Australia in Hyderabad and the first-ever ODI double century against South Africa in Gwalior. Tendulkar called it the “super bat”.
Tendulkar also recalled his father’s advice about what a cricket bat meant to a player, urging him to keep the equipment close to him.
“My father used to say that you should keep your things close to you. That includes your talent. It’s a God’s gift. So you have to keep it close and worship it,” he said. “Why should you throw a bat? What are you going to achieve? Why disrespect your gift?”
The collection also included his first helmet, Mumbai’s Ranji Trophy jersey, the India jersey and helmet from his 200th Test, and the sheet of paper on which he wrote the points for his farewell speech at Wankhede Stadium.

briefs.headline: Shubman Gill's hunger and appetite to improve set him apart: Williamson
briefs.deck: Shubman Gill arrived early with Gurnoor Brar, and Kane Williamson arranged a camp for his former Gujarat Titans teammate before the ODI series got underway. In an exclusive conversation with TOI, Williamson, who has released his autobiography, "The Bare Margins", opens up about his bond with Gill and the two-Test series.
briefs.bodyText:
WELLINGTON: 
Kane Williamson
 has been 
Shubman Gill
's go-to man before every important overseas Test assignment. The Indian captain reached out to him before the tour of England last year and repeated the drill before arriving in New Zealand. While the English summer involved conversations about technical adjustments, last month's focus in Auckland was on getting acclimatised to the conditions.
Gill arrived early with Gurnoor Brar, and Williamson arranged a camp for his former Gujarat Titans teammate before the ODI series got underway. In an exclusive conversation with TOI, Williamson, who has released his autobiography, "The Bare Margins", opens up about his bond with Gill and the two-Test series.
Excerpts:You are on Shubman Gill's speed dial before he travels for a Test series. How has discussing batting with him been?
Look, he is a lovely human being and a proper student of the game. Our relationship goes back a long way, from our time together at Gujarat Titans, and he keeps reaching out from time to time to discuss batting. We have had numerous conversations about the different nuances of the game, and his appetite to grow and improve as a batter is commendable.
Did he reach out before coming to New Zealand too?
He arrived early in Auckland and wanted to start preparing well before the long series. So I helped arrange a few days of practice for him to ensure he got some work in before the series started. He constantly wants to improve, so it's no surprise that his career is on an upward curve. As I said, his hunger and appetite to constantly improve set him apart.
Gill had a very good series in England. Do you think New Zealand will be the most challenging tour of his career?
He had a very good series in England, both he and the team. And I am really excited to see him bat in these conditions. He is a world-class batter, and I am sure he will enjoy batting here. The conditions are challenging for any visiting team, but I am sure he will be up for the task when the series gets underway.
There's a lot of chatter about the wind in Wellington from a bowling standpoint. But is the challenge equally stiff for batters?
Well, yes (laughs). The crosswinds can sometimes blow you off your stance, so you need to be ready for that. You also need to factor in which way the wind is blowing because if it's against the bowler, deliveries from one end can come slower than from the other. And batters from both teams will face that challenge. But it's about getting used to it quickly and just factoring in the direction. For bowlers, it's going to be a bigger challenge, and I expect Mohammed Siraj from India to do the heavy lifting because he is the kind of character who bowls with a big heart and can bowl long spells.
What would your advice be to batters from both teams?
Balance is key. If a batter remains nice and balanced, especially when the spell of crosswinds begins, it should be fine. I wouldn't say there is a need for other changes. Just balance and staying nice and steady at the crease are important.
Both teams have potent bowling attacks, and we saw a trailer of that in the ODI series. But will this series be more about how well the batters perform?
I feel the conditions will be more or less similar across the two venues. There will be nice bounce, carry and movement on offer for the bowlers, but there will be periods when the surfaces ease out. There will be that initial help for the bowlers, as there always has been, but both teams also have enough quality in their batting groups.
How did you get the idea to pen your cricket journey into a book, The Bare Margins?
Well, I wasn't really keen initially, but my friend convinced me to do it. And it was really exciting to pen down my thoughts honestly, and it felt like a full circle for me. Obviously, I have mentioned my journey, New Zealand's cricket journey, the role of Brendon McCullum and many other things, as honestly as I could.

briefs.headline: What next for Rohit? NZ struggles, advancing age put veteran's place under scrutiny
briefs.deck: The debate is now unavoidable: should Rohit play the 2027 World Cup? And are India running out of time to prepare alternatives if his form does not improve?
briefs.bodyText:
The batting conditions in India's five-match ODI series against New Zealand, which ended on Sunday, were far from straightforward, especially under lights. The ball moved in the air and off the pitch, while the tennis-ball bounce gave pacers plenty to work with.
Even so, 
Rohit Sharma
's returns were stark: 0 off 6, 23 off 28, 0 off 1 and 7 off 13. Looking leaden-footed on seamer-friendly surfaces and far removed from the batter who has scored 12,150 runs in 296 ODIs at 48.60, with 35 centuries, 63 fifties and a world-record 264, the 39-year-old managed just 30 runs in four innings at 7.50.
For a player who has dominated ODI cricket since moving to the top of the order in 2013, such a lean run is rare. This was his 26th overseas ODI series across nearly two decades, and only the third in which he averaged in single digits. On three occasions, he has averaged more than 100.
The only time he fared worse across at least four innings was against Sri Lanka 14 years ago, a series he later described as the worst of his career. Rohit made just 13 runs in five matches, averaging 2.60. Rohit's dismissals in New Zealand exposed his struggles against the moving ball. 
He fell to Jamieson in Auckland and Wellington, edged Matt Henry at Mount Maunganui and picked out midwicket off Matthew Fisher in his final innings.
With the 2027 ODI World Cup approaching, every failure will fuel the age debate. Rohit was 39 years and 199 days old in his last ODI and will be 40 years and 180 days old when India face Australia in their World Cup opener in Cape Town. Every lean series will inevitably raise questions about his place in the team.
He will have opportunities to regain form in the home ODI series against Sri Lanka, beginning in Vi-zag on Dec 13, and Zimbabwe, starting in Kolkata on Jan 3, 2027. Howe-ver, India's batting-friendly pitches may not test his reflexes as seve-rely as New Zealand's conditions.
Rohit's struggles have brought India's alternatives into focus, with young openers 
Yashasvi Jaiswal
, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Abhishek Sharma waiting for opportunities. Jaiswal, in particular, has been unlucky, having scored 285 runs at 71.25, including two centuries, in just six ODIs but struggled to find a regular place behind Rohit and Shubman Gill.
The debate is now unavoidable: should Rohit play the 2027 World Cup? And are India running out of time to prepare alternatives if his form does not improve?
There is a cautionary precedent in MS Dhoni's final phase. The former India captain, an all-time white-ball great, found it increasingly difficult to force the pace during the 2019 World Cup in England, where India exited in the semifinals. Will Rohit's final lap follow a similar path, or can he rediscover his touch and sign off on his own terms?
It is no secret that the selectors had initially looked beyond Rohit for the 2027 World Cup and indicated that Lord's could be his final appearance in India colours. However, the Mumbaikar convinced the BCCI hierarchy of his worth and his desire to continue until the global event.
That raises another question: was former chief selector and India pacer 
Ajit Agarkar
 right to question Rohit's place in the ODI side, even as the BCCI backed the superstar's World Cup ambitions? The reported disagreement between the two only sharpened the issue.
Much will now depend on how the new selection committee, headed by former left-arm spinner Pragyan Ojha, views Rohit's form and future. Ojha, a former India and Mumbai Indians teammate of Rohit, will face a difficult call if the batter's lean run continues. Selection meetings are also attended by Centre of Excellence chairperson and former India batter VVS Laxman.
There is precedent for selectors making tough calls on established stars. During his tenure as chief selector from 2012 to 2016, former India batter Sandeep Patil oversaw the transition away from several greats, most notably Sachin Tendulkar.
Patil, however, believes Rohit deserves time to regain form and has backed him to make the World Cup squad. "Rohit and Virat are the kind of players whose class is permanent. Form is temporary. Not scoring runs in a series can happen. What is more important is the 2027 ODI World Cup, not this ODI series in New Zealand. As a big fan of Rohit, I would love to see him in the World Cup, but the decision remains with the selectors and Rohit," Patil told TOI on Monday.
He said there was still almost a year to go before the tournament, giving Rohit time to recover, provided he stayed fit and competitive.

briefs.headline: 'We will play four fast bowlers': Shubman Gill ahead of first Test vs NZ
briefs.deck: India's captain Shubman Gill announced the team's plan to field four fast bowlers in the upcoming Test. The series against New Zealand poses a bigger challenge compared to the recently concluded ODI series. Jasprit Bumrah is expected to lead the pace attack with several other bowlers competing for spots. Meanwhile, Gill expressed confidence in wicketkeeper-batter Rishabh Pant's abilities despite…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India captain 
Shubman Gill
 has confirmed that the team will play four fast bowlers in the first Test against New Zealand, starting November 19 in Wellington.
With several players competing for places in the playing XI, Gill said the team was still working on its final combination. However, he made it clear that India would rely on four pacers for the series opener at the Basin Reserve.
"We have a good headache… fast bowlers stepped up in ODI series. We are still deciding on final combination. We will play with four fast bowlers," Gill told reporters.
He also explained the team's batting and bowling options while discussing the possible playing XI.
"We will have seven batters, 8-9 we have Anshul and Akash who can bat a bit. So still deciding, Nitish can bat. We need to factor in when ball goes old, so need someone who can hit deck hard," he said.
Jasprit Bumrah is likely to lead India's pace attack, with Akash Deep, Mohammed Siraj and Prasidh Krishna also in the squad.
Gurnoor Brar has also been added to India's squad for the two-Test series, while left-arm wrist-spinner Kuldeep Yadav has been released. The decision to include more pacers comes with India expecting seam-friendly conditions in New Zealand.
'New Zealand have good record here'
Gill expects the Test series to be a bigger challenge for India than the recently concluded ODI series.
"This is going to be bigger challenge than ODIs, New Zealand have good record here. Will be exciting," he said.
Gill backs Rishabh Pant
The India captain also backed wicketkeeper-batter Rishabh Pant, who has been dealing with fitness issues.
Gill highlighted Pant's experience and his record of scoring centuries in different conditions around the world.
"He is one of the most experienced player in the team. He has scored 100s all over the world," Gill said.

briefs.headline: 'Donkey work' awaits Bumrah & Co: Shane Bond, Kyle Mills on Wellington's wind challenge
briefs.deck: In simpler terms, a fast bowler has to be prepared to run into the wind and put in the hard yards for extended periods during a Test match. Former New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond says both Wellington and Christchurch are windy cities, but the strength of the wind makes the former a little more challenging. He expects someone to do the "donkey work" for an extended period when the action gets…
briefs.bodyText:
WELLINGTON: India's first stop in the two-match Test series will be the Basin Reserve in 'Windy Welly'. The entire squad, except 
Mohammed Siraj
, has been training in the city since November 12 and will have two more sessions before taking the field for the series opener. The Basin Reserve is a challenging venue for any visiting team because of its open surroundings and strong winds, which usually blow straight down from one end.
In simpler terms, a fast bowler has to be prepared to run into the wind and put in the hard yards for extended periods during a Test match. Former New Zealand fast bowler 
Shane Bond
 says both Wellington and Christchurch are windy cities, but the strength of the wind makes the former a little more challenging. He expects someone to do the "donkey work" for an extended period when the action gets underway on November 19.
"Christchurch is a windy town too. The biggest thing probably, the difference between Christchurch and Wellington is when the wind blows, it's the strength of the wind and it generally blows straight down from one end. So someone's going to have to do some donkey work into it. I've seen in the past that even if you're a first-class bowler at home, having to bowl into the wind at Wellington can present some real problems.
 Particularly if you bowl downwind for your state team and then have to run into the wind at Wellington. It is a specialised role. It can be challenging if the wind's up there," Bond tells TOI in an exclusive chat.
The 51-year-old, who was on broadcast duties during the limited-overs series and is now busy with his ILT20 commitments, says there are calm days too, but teams should expect at least a couple of days when they will have to contend with strong gusts. When India played a T20I here, players found it difficult to keep their gear in place, with caps, sunglasses and other equipment repeatedly flying away. Can players prepare for such conditions, even if they arrive early? Bond doesn't think so.
"It's usually not like that for five days. But over the course of a Test match, you'd be expecting a day or two where the wind's pretty strong. It's pretty tough to prepare for. Most of the guys now, international cricketers, have played all over the world in all sorts of different conditions," says Bond.
The weather in New Zealand has been largely pleasant during the day and chilly in the evening. More of the same is expected in Wellington over the next week, but players need to be ready for a demanding workout as the "wind can be draining".
"New Zealand's not a particularly hot country, but the wind can be draining. You end up getting short spells into the wind from one end. Your spinner often does a bulk of the donkey work. So your fast bowlers, especially your attacking ones, rotate from one end downwind. You're trying to find a couple of bowlers who do the bulk of that work into the wind if it's strong," adds Bond.
November is not the usual time for the start of a Test series in New Zealand, and former fast bowler 
Kyle Mills
 says the country experiences stronger winds during the period leading up to Christmas. He feels for the bowler who will have to run into the wind at the Basin Reserve this week.
"What tends to happen here in New Zealand in the spring, before Christmas, are more windy periods. We get a lot of strong winds, and Wellington traditionally has a lot of strong winds anyway. There's going to be an unfortunate bowler who's going to be bowling into the wind. In Wellington, you can't dodge that at all. But I think with both pitches, you're still going to get good pace and carry through to the wicketkeeper. You will get a little bit of swing," says Mills.
The likes of Jasprit Bumrah, Anshul Kamboj, Gurnoor Brar, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep and Mohammed Siraj have spent enough time in New Zealand to become accustomed to the conditions. But come November 19, a date that holds painful memories in the Indian cricket calendar, it will be about who comes out on top in the battle against the wind.

briefs.headline: New Zealand suffer major injury blow ahead of India Test series
briefs.deck: Mitchell Santner has been ruled out of the upcoming Test series against India due to a hand fracture. His injury occurred while batting in the fifth ODI against India, confirmed by scans. Dean Foxcroft has been named as his replacement in the Test squad led by Tom Latham. New Zealand Cricket will provide updates regarding Santner's recovery timeline later.
briefs.bodyText:
New Zealand have suffered a major setback ahead of their two-Test series against India, with experienced all-rounder 
Mitchell Santner
 ruled out due to a fracture in his right hand.
Santner, who is New Zealand's white-ball captain, suffered the injury while batting in the fifth and final ODI against India on Sunday. Scans later confirmed the fracture.
"Scans have revealed that Santner has fractured his right-hand. His return-to-play timeline is being worked through and his involvement in the Test series to Australia will be updated in due course," the release said.
Dean Foxcroft named as Santner's replacement
Central Districts spin-bowling all-rounder Dean Foxcroft has been called up to replace Santner in the Tom Latham-led Test squad.
"Central Districts spin-bowling all-rounder Dean Foxcroft, who made his Test debut against Ireland in May, has been called into the squad to replace Santner," the release said.
Foxcroft made his Test debut against Ireland in May.
New Zealand face India in two-Test series
New Zealand Cricket is still assessing Santner's recovery timeline. An update on his availability for the Test series against Australia, which follows the India assignment, will be provided later.
The first Test against India will be played at the Basin Reserve in Wellington from Thursday. The second Test will be held at Hagley Oval in Christchurch from November 27.
New Zealand have also struggled with injuries during the ODI series against India. Several key players missed matches as the hosts lost the five-match series 1-3.

briefs.headline: 'Dravid batted us into submission': Mills recalls India's 2009 triumph
briefs.deck: Kyle Mills, who took a solitary wicket in the match, still remembers getting Team India head coach Gautam Gambhir out leg before wicket, but he had overstepped, which gave the southpaw an early reprieve. Mills feels it could have been a different story had they taken the early wicket, but it wasn't meant to be.
briefs.bodyText:
WELLINGTON: New Zealand has always remained a tricky frontier for India. It's been 17 years since India last won a Test match in New Zealand. Even India's famous win at Seddon Park in Hamilton in 2009, which sealed a memorable series victory for the MS Dhoni-led side, came 33 years after the previous Test series win in New Zealand.
Kyle Mills
, part of the New Zealand squad for the Hamilton fixture, vividly, but not fondly, remembers the game as his last outing for the Black Caps in whites.
"I remember that Test very well. That Test match was the epitome of the 
Rahul Dravid
 ‘Wall’. He batted beautifully and really dug in, batting us into submission. That was actually my last Test match, so not fond memories," Mills recalled in an interview with TOI.
The Kiwi seamer, who took a solitary wicket in the match, still remembers getting Team India head coach Gautam Gambhir out leg before wicket, but he had overstepped, which gave the southpaw an early reprieve. Mills feels it could have been a different story had they taken the early wicket, but it wasn't meant to be.
"I actually got Gambhir out LBW; well, it was out, it was absolutely dead out, but my front foot was over the line, and Simon Taufel was the umpire and called me for a no ball, and then I was gutted because it would have been great to get an early wicket, and then who knows how the game would have progressed," says Mills.
Gambhir scored 72 and partnered solidly with Rahul Dravid, and the two set a solid platform for the Little Master 
Sachin Tendulkar
 to dominate from. Tendulkar scored a brilliant 160, and his 260-ball essay was enough to bat the hosts out of the game.
"Rahul Dravid was amazing in that Test match, so was Sachin Tendulkar. You kind of think about some of the players you had in that series... Zaheer Khan was playing; they're generational cricketing greats, (Virender) Sehwag played that Test, (VVS) Laxman was also there. India had a brilliant cricket team during that period and potentially played as well... just a brilliant cricket team," adds Mills.
Sachin Tendulkar scored a brilliant 160, and his 260-ball essay was enough to bat the hosts out of the game. (AFP Photo)
The fixture turned out to be a cruel ending for Mills in more ways than one, as he also conceded the winning runs off Gambhir's bat in the second innings when India stormed home without losing a wicket.
The former India opener now returns to the familiar territory but with a different challenge, and without the bat in hand. For Mills, Gambhir remains the "tough competitor" unwilling to drop an inch.
"He's always a tough competitor on the field, without question. No jokes were going around at all because he was always business on the field, a tough cricketer. Post-cricket, he got into politics and became a leader. He is obviously a great tactician, was a wonderful player, very professional across all facets of the game, and a tough taskmaster as well," concludes Mills.

briefs.headline: Lakshya Sen roars back to life
briefs.deck: After months of frustration, tough losses and a season that threatened to slip away, the ace shuttler has found his mojo again, winning back-to-back titles at the Hylo Open and Japan Masters to boost his BWF World Tour Finals hopes
briefs.bodyText:
Some rallies are remembered for the winner. Others, for the sheer audacity of keeping the shuttle alive when the point seems all but lost. Lakshya Sen’s late-season resurgence has been a little like that. Just when his 2026 campaign appeared to be running out of steam, the Indian found a way to keep the rally going.
From the unforgiving pace of Germany to the hostile home-court atmosphere in Japan, Lakshya won 10 matches in succession, lifting the Hylo Open and Kumamoto Masters Japan titles. It is the manner of the victories that has made this November run so exhilarating. He has out-powered a towering Frenchman, outmanoeuvred one of Indonesia’s most promising young shuttlers and outlasted a Japanese opponent in front of a partisan crowd. The familiar aggression is back. So, too, is the roar.

briefs.headline: ‘Best sleep of my life’: Ashwin opens up on dismissing Jos Buttler in IPL 2019
briefs.bodyText:
R Ashwin got embroiled in a controversy in IPL 2019 in a match between then Kings XI Punjab and Rajasthan Royals when he mankaded RR’s Jos Buttler. The incident had raised a lot of controversy on fair play. Since then, the controversy has always followed Ashwin everywhere and he recently opened up on it in a chat with former India batter Aakash Chopra.
“In that game, Rajasthan Royals had an edge. I was the captain of Kings XI. I had done the run out and my team got upset. I called everyone and said these people were disturbed. I knew in the next three days, I would have to listen to everyone give their opinion on the run out. But I would handle it. Our task was to win the game and that we won. If Buttler’s run out gives us the victory and 2 points, why shouldn’t we take it?,” Ashwin said in the Baith and Bol show on Chopra’s YouTube channel.
“People kept saying I waited intentionally to get the run out. Not my fault. Umpire has to see if by law it’s out or not. If I waited for Buttler to get out of his crease, he should have also waited for me to release the ball. That’s also not my fault. If this dismissal is illegal, MCC should look into it. It’s not my fault so why should I feel bad? I went back, had good dessert and had the best sleep of my life,” he added.
R Ashwin recounts the Jos Buttler runout at the non-striker’s end. What is legal must also be ethical.

— Aakash Chopra (@cricketaakash) November 16, 2026
In the match, chasing a target of 185, the Royals had started off well with Buttler flashing his bat superbly until Ashwin took the bails off before even delivering his ball to dismiss the batsman.
The pair had exchanged words after the incident, where Buttler was clearly out of the crease. It took the third umpire to declare an outright dismissal which changed the course of the match. KXIP went on to register a 14-run win over Rajasthan Royals, who were restricted to 170 for nine in the chase.
3 years later, the pair of Ashwin and Buttler would end their bitter feud when both played for the Rajasthan Royals when the spinner was bought by the franchise in the IPL 2022 mega auction.
In 2022, the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) announced its new code of laws, accepted Mankading (or Browned, as Sunil Gavaskar calls it) as a normal mode of running out the non-striker, removing it from Law 41 (Unfair play) and clubbing it with Law 38 (Run out).
